extracted.intended_audience: general readers, science fiction and fantasy writers and fans (including SFWA members)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the Nebula Awards' eligibility, categories, nomination and voting rules, and related honorary awards as described on the Wikipedia page. Useful for writers and readers who need to know what works qualify and how the awards process works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication language and location eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for consideration works must be published in English in the United States. Works published in English elsewhere in the world are also eligible provided they are released on either a website or in an electronic edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline eligibility rule for the Nebula Awards as stated; publication must be in English and either physically published in the U.S. or (if published elsewhere) available as a website or electronic edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translated works eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Works translated into English are eligible for the Nebula Awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations into English are explicitly allowed; the page does not add further limitations here (e.g., on translator credit or first-English-publication timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author nationality and SFWA membership not required
rubrics_metrics.description: The awards are not limited to American citizens or members of SFWA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any author may have works considered so long as the work itself meets the publication/language eligibility rules; nomination and voting, however, are member-driven (see nomination rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre qualification left to nominators and voters
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no written rules as to which works qualify as science fiction or fantasy; the decision of eligibility in that regard is left up to the nominators and voters, rather than to SFWA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SF or fantasy classification is intentionally flexible and determined by the voting body, not by a fixed SFWA definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award year identification
rubrics_metrics.description: SFWA identifies the awards by the year of publication, that is, the year prior to the year in which the award is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners are referenced by the publication year of the work (e.g., the '2025 Nebula' would refer to works published in 2025 though the ceremony occurs the following year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Novel — length definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Novel: Stories of 40,000 words or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numeric word-count threshold defines what qualifies as a novel for Nebula categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Novella — length definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Novella: Stories of between 17,500 and 40,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works whose word counts fall within this range are eligible in the Novella category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Novelette — length definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Novelette: Stories of between 7,500 and 17,500 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category covers mid-length short fiction between short story and novella limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Short Story — length definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Short Story: Stories of less than 7,500 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flash and short pieces under 7,500 words are eligible in this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Script (historical category) — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Script: Movie or television episode scripts (presented 1974–1978, 2000–2009).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category has existed during specific periods; after 2009 it was removed and replaced by the Ray Bradbury Award (see related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Andre Norton Award (middle grade & YA fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Andre Norton Award: Middle grade and young adult fiction (inaugurated in 2006; promoted to an official Nebula category in 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally a separate award, it is now treated as an official Nebula category for YA/MG works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ray Bradbury Award (dramatic presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ray Bradbury Award: Outstanding Dramatic Presentation / Dramatic presentations (replacing the Best Script in 2010 and promoted to official Nebula status later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers dramatic presentations (scripts/other dramatic media); its relationship to the Nebula ballot has changed over time and was incorporated as an official Nebula award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Game Writing — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Game Writing: Writing in video and tabletop games (category added in 2018).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes narrative and writing specifically for games (both video and tabletop formats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Comics — scope (2026 addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Comics: Writing in comics (added as a Nebula category in 2026).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers comic writing; added to the official set of Nebula categories starting in 2026.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Poetry — scope (2026 addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best Poetry: Writing in poetry (added as a Nebula category in 2026).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes poetic works in speculative genres; introduced as a Nebula category in 2026.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination eligibility and window
rubrics_metrics.description: Works are nominated each year between November 15 and February 15 by published authors who are members of the organization (SFWA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only published-author SFWA members may nominate, and nominations must be made within the specified annual window (Nov 15–Feb 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final ballot formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The six works that receive the most nominations form the final ballot. Additional nominees are possible in the case of ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top six nomination-getters become finalists; ties can expand the final ballot beyond six entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting period and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Members then vote on the ballot throughout March, and the final results are presented at the Nebula Awards ceremony in May.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the nomination window closes, SFWA members cast final votes in March; winners announced at the spring ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-nomination and nomination decline rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are not permitted to nominate their own works, though they can decline nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-nomination is prohibited; an author who is nominated may opt to decline being on the ballot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie-breaking in final vote
rubrics_metrics.description: Ties in the final vote are broken, if possible, by the number of nominations the works received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a final vote results in a tie, the work with more original nominations (from the nominating phase) wins if that breaks the tie.

rubrics_metrics.name: "No Award" voting option
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1970 voters have had the option to select 'no award' if they felt that no nominated work was worthy of winning; this has been used in some categories historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voters may explicitly choose 'no award' on the final ballot, and when 'no award' wins the category is not awarded that year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility-year/calendar-year rule and rolling eligibility history
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning in 1980 the eligibility year for nominations was set to the calendar year (rather than a December–November window). Prior to 2009 the Nebulas employed a rolling eligibility system in which each work was eligible to qualify for the ballot for one year following its date of publication; beginning with the 2010 awards the rolling eligibility system and paperback-publication exemption were replaced with the current rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility timing has changed over the history of the awards; currently (post-2010) the calendar-year based system is in use and rolling eligibility has been discontinued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize form — trophy, no cash prize
rubrics_metrics.description: The winner receives a trophy but no cash prize; the trophy is a transparent block with an embedded glitter spiral nebula and gemstones cut to resemble planets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition is in the form of a physical trophy and the prestige of the award; there is no monetary award attached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary honorary awards and their purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Beside the Nebulas, several other awards and honors are presented at the Nebula Awards ceremony: the Damon Knight Memorial Grand Master Award (since 1975) for 'lifetime achievement in science fiction and/or fantasy', the Author Emeritus (since 1995; not awarded since 2014) for contributions to the field, the Kevin O'Donnell, Jr. Award for service to SFWA, the Kate Wilhelm Solstice Award (since 2009) for significant impact on speculative fiction, and the Infinity Award (since 2023) as a posthumous equivalent to the Grand Master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These honors are discretionary (not competitively nominated/voted in the same way as the Nebula categories); note specific rules such as the Solstice Award may be presented posthumously whereas Grand Master and Author Emeritus historically are living-only (Grand Master named most years but two since 1995).
